//: The boundary of the certified item: which kernel source files are inside
the thing a certificate would attach to, which are the uncertified load
above it, and which are verification rather than product.
Enforced by scripts/check-item-boundary.py and explained in
docs/certification/ITEM.md. Every assurance artifact in docs/certification
is scoped to this file: the Security Target's TOE, the hazard analysis's
safety item, the traceability matrix and the coverage obligation all mean
'the rings named here'. Move a file between rings and you have changed
what four ratings are claims about, which is why it is a diff somebody has
to argue for rather than a directory convention.
Three rings, nested, tightest first. The point of the nesting is that the
boundary can ratchet inward without re-scoping the scheme: raising the
target from EAL5+ to EAL6+, or from SIL 2 to ASIL D, is then a matter of
moving modules from 'item' to 'core', not of rewriting the artifacts.
A file in no ring fails the build. That is the ratchet's teeth: a new
kernel module cannot drift into the item by being written, and cannot
drift out of the analysis by being forgotten.
A certificate attaches to a configuration, not to a repository. This is
the one under evaluation: three architectures, release profile, the
gate set cargo xtask check runs, and the toolchain rust-toolchain.toml
pins. Seven Cargo features exist in the whole workspace and none is in
kernel/ or boot/, so there is no configuration space to enumerate --
which is most of why this item is analysable at all.

//test_file_patterns: In-kernel self-tests: the code behind 'every boot proves its own claims'.
Product code and verification code are counted apart everywhere in the
assurance argument, because a standard asks quite different questions of
each -- the first has to be covered by tests, the second *is* the test.
Roughly a quarter of kernel/ is this. Excluding it from the item's size
is not a way of looking smaller: these files are cited as verification
evidence in docs/certification/VERIFICATION.md, where they have to earn

core.status: aspirational -- the ratchet's destination, not a current claim
why: The minimal trusted computing base: the code that must be correct for
memory protection, scheduling and capability enforcement to mean
anything. Nothing here may depend on a filesystem, a network stack or
a device driver, and that is checked rather than intended.
This ring is what a later EAL6+ or ASIL D effort would evaluate. It is
named now, while it is cheap to name, because the cost of discovering
a boundary later is every artifact written against the wrong one.

item.status: the boundary the current artifacts are written against
why: The core, plus the code that brings it up, dispatches into it and
enumerates the hardware it hands to ring 3. This is the item all four
present ratings attach to.
The native ABI is here rather than in the core because it is the
interface the item exports, and an interface is evaluated with the
thing that exports it. The Linux personality is deliberately *not*
here: it is a compatibility obligation over which the project has no
design authority, its syscall surface is the largest single body of
code in the kernel, and none of it has to be correct for isolation to
hold. That is the whole argument for the boundary sitting where it
does.
Device enumeration is inside; device drivers are not. The kernel walks
ACPI, the device tree and PCI because that needs privilege, then hands
an IoMapping and an IOMMU domain to a ring-3 driver. scripts/
check-device-access.py already holds that seam for the code; this
holds it for the certificate.
Everything the item runs but does not vouch for. A defect here is
bounded by the item's own enforcement: a ring-3 driver fault is a
process fault, and a Linux-personality defect cannot reach an address
space the core did not hand it.
This is not a list of code that matters less. It is the filesystem,
the network stack and the compatibility layer -- most of what makes
Ferrix useful. It is excluded because a claim over 93,714 lines of
product code is a claim nobody can afford to substantiate, and one
over ~40,000 is a claim that can be.

dependency_rules.why: A trusted computing base that reaches upward is not one.
The item may be called by the load above it, and may not call into it. Where it must -- init has to start a filesystem -- the call goes through an interface the item defines, not a module it names.

//: References that break a dependency rule today, each one a finding in
docs/certification/FINDINGS.md. The list exists so the gate can go into
CI green and ratchet down; it is a debt register, not an exemption
mechanism. Every entry needs a finding id, and the gate fails if the
list grows or if an entry goes stale.
Populated by running the gate. An empty list here on a tree that has
never been measured would be a lie told by omission.
